title: Explain animal classification and natural history

lessons.title: How animals are classified
lessons.html:
Why classify animals?

Scientists group living things according to shared features and evolutionary relationships. This system, called taxonomy, gives every species one scientific name that is understood worldwide. For a farm supervisor this matters because breed registers, veterinary products, research and disease regulations all use scientific names, and because related animals often share diseases, digestive systems and behaviour.

The levels of classification

From broadest to most specific, the main levels (taxa) are:

  1. Kingdom
  2. Phylum
  3. Class
  4. Order
  5. Family
  6. Genus
  7. Species

A memory aid is: King Philip Came Over For Good Soup.

Example: domestic cattle

LevelGroup
KingdomAnimalia (animals)
PhylumChordata (animals with a spinal cord)
ClassMammalia (mammals)
OrderArtiodactyla (even-toed hoofed animals)
FamilyBovidae (cattle, sheep, goats, antelope)
GenusBos
SpeciesBos taurus (European-type cattle) and Bos indicus (humped zebu-type cattle)

Binomial names

The scientific name has two parts, genus and species, written in italics with a capital letter only on the genus, for example Ovis aries (sheep), Capra hircus (goat), Sus scrofa (pig), Gallus gallus (chicken) and Equus caballus (horse). This system was set up by Carl Linnaeus in the 1700s.

Species and breeds

A species is a group whose members can breed together and produce fertile offspring. A breed is a group within a species that humans have selected for certain traits. Bonsmara, Nguni and Afrikaner are breeds of cattle; Dorper and Merino are breeds of sheep. Different breeds of one species can be crossed freely, while crosses between species, such as a horse and a donkey, usually give sterile offspring like the mule.

lessons.title: Major animal groups important to agriculture
lessons.html:
Vertebrates and invertebrates

Animals are divided broadly into vertebrates, which have a backbone, and invertebrates, which do not. Both groups matter on a farm.

Vertebrate classes

  • Mammals - hair, warm-blooded, feed young on milk. Cattle, sheep, goats, pigs, horses, rabbits, and also wildlife such as kudu and springbok, and predators such as the jackal and caracal.
  • Birds - feathers, warm-blooded, lay eggs. Chickens, ostriches, ducks, and wild birds that may spread avian influenza.
  • Reptiles - scales, cold-blooded. Snakes such as the puff adder and Cape cobra are a hazard to workers and stock.
  • Amphibians - frogs and toads; moist skin, life cycle partly in water.
  • Fish - gills; relevant in aquaculture such as tilapia and trout farming.

Groups among farm mammals

  • Ruminants (cattle, sheep, goats, antelope) - four-part stomach, chew the cud.
  • Non-ruminant herbivores (horses, rabbits) - hindgut fermentation.
  • Omnivores (pigs) - eat plant and animal material, simple stomach.

Invertebrates on the farm

  • Arthropods - insects (bees, flies, locusts) and arachnids (ticks, mites, spiders). Ticks spread redwater and heartwater; blowflies cause fly strike.
  • Nematodes (roundworms) - such as wireworm in sheep.
  • Flatworms - tapeworms and liver fluke.
  • Molluscs - snails, some of which carry liver fluke larvae.

Knowing which group a parasite belongs to helps choose control methods. Remedies that kill roundworms may not work on tapeworms or fluke, so always read the label and follow vet advice.

Classification also helps with disease risk. Closely related animals often share diseases: antelope and cattle are both bovids and can share diseases such as foot-and-mouth disease, and wild birds can carry avian influenza to poultry. This is why game and livestock interfaces are carefully managed.

lessons.title: Natural history, domestication and behaviour
lessons.html:
Natural history

Natural history is the study of how animals live in nature: their habitat, food, social behaviour, breeding and how they adapted to their environment. Domestic animals still carry the behaviour of their wild ancestors, and good stockmen use this.

Domestication

Humans domesticated animals over thousands of years by keeping and breeding the tamest and most useful individuals.

  • Cattle descend from the wild aurochs. Sanga-type cattle such as the Nguni and Afrikaner came to southern Africa with migrating peoples centuries ago and adapted to local ticks, heat and veld.
  • Sheep descend from wild mouflon-type sheep, and goats from the wild bezoar goat.
  • Pigs descend from the wild boar.
  • Chickens descend from the red junglefowl of Asia.

Adaptation

Natural selection favours animals suited to their environment. Indigenous breeds show this: Nguni cattle have tick resistance and tolerate heat; the fat-tailed and fat-rumped sheep store energy for dry times; the Boer goat browses bush that cattle cannot use. Selecting adapted breeds lowers costs for dips, feed and veterinary care.

Behaviour that comes from the wild

  • Herd and flock instinct - prey animals feel safe in groups and panic when isolated. Move them in groups.
  • Flight zone - each animal has a personal space. Entering it makes the animal move away; this is the basis of low-stress handling.
  • Hierarchy - groups have a pecking order. Mixing strange animals causes fighting, so mix carefully.
  • Maternal behaviour - mothers hide or defend young. Cows with new calves can attack.
  • Predator-prey relationship - jackal, caracal and feral dogs prey on small stock. Understanding their habits helps plan kraaling at night and other damage control.

Key points

  • Classification runs from kingdom to species; scientific names have genus and species.
  • A species interbreeds to produce fertile offspring; a breed is a selected group within a species.
  • Farm animals are mostly mammals and birds; many parasites are arthropods and worms.
  • Domestic animals keep wild behaviour such as herding and flight zones.
  • Indigenous breeds are adapted to local conditions.
